oni.desc: The Oceanic Niño Index — 3-month running mean of Niño 3.4 SST anomalies, the official ENSO yardstick. +0.5°C sustained = El Niño; +2.0°C = very strong.
oni.inference: The ONI (3-month mean) reached roughly +2.46°C for JAS 2026 on IRI's reckoning and is still climbing toward the autumn–winter peak — a trajectory steeper than 1997 or 2015 at the equivalent stage, and now firmly in very-strong territory months before the maximum. Because it is a 3-month mean it lags the weekly Niño 3.4 (which hit +3.3°C on October 14), so the official index will keep rising. The question is no longer whether this is a major event but whether it sets an outright record.

roni.desc: The Relative ONI strips out the tropical ocean's background warming. CPC now frames the historic-event threshold in RONI terms: ≥+2.5°C on the 3-month RONI would exceed any event since 1950.
roni.inference: RONI is the index that settles the record question, and CPC has sharpened it: an 83% chance the 3-month RONI reaches ≥+2.5°C during Oct–Dec (up from 75% in September), which would exceed every El Niño back to 1950, with 54% for Sep–Nov and 70% for Nov–Jan. The relative index is running at or above the traditional ONI — a sign of how strong the Niño signal is against the already-warm baseline. Both indices are climbing steeply together; the debate is only how far above +2.5°C RONI the peak reaches.

nino34.desc: Niño 3.4 SST anomaly. The JAS seasonal was +2.46°C; the weekly index centred on October 14 reached +3.3°C. Eastern-basin Niño-1+2 hit +3.9°C and Niño-3 +3.0°C (September monthly).
nino34.inference: The weekly Niño 3.4 reached +3.3°C by mid-October and the IRI multimodel average projects a peak near +3.5°C in OND–NDJ, with about 10 of 27 models at or above +3.5°C — beyond IRI's highest defined category. The structure is intensely east-weighted: Niño-1+2 at +3.9°C and Niño-3 at +3.0°C mark extraordinary eastern-Pacific and South-American-coast warmth, the signature of the most intense events (1982-83, 1997-98). This is the chart driving the record conversation.

subsurface.desc: Warm Water Volume anomaly — the subsurface heat reservoir fuelling surface warming. CPC (Oct 8): the equatorial subsurface index (180°–100°W) is well above average, reflecting a deeper-than-average thermocline.
subsurface.inference: The subsurface reservoir remains well above average with a deeper-than-average thermocline, continuing to feed the surface as the event approaches its peak. The eastern-Pacific warmth has if anything deepened since September. With no sign of premature discharge, the reservoir still supports further surface warming through the OND–NDJ maximum — the physical basis for the near-+3.5°C peak the models project.

atmosphere.desc: The Southern Oscillation Index and low-level winds confirm coupling. The SOI reached −21.4 in September and −18.6 on the latest 30-day value (through Oct 17); the traditional and equatorial SOI remain significantly negative.
atmosphere.inference: Ocean–atmosphere coupling is firmly established and deeply negative. The SOI was −21.4 in September and −18.6 on the latest 30-day value — a pronounced, sustained weakening of the Walker circulation. Enhanced convection spans the central-to-eastern Pacific while suppression persists over Indonesia; low-level westerlies extend across the basin. This is a mature, self-reinforcing Bjerknes feedback carrying the event into its peak with no hint of decoupling.

regime.name: ENSO Regime Score
regime.interp: Very strong and all but certainly historic. CPC: 83% chance of exceeding any event since 1950 on RONI; multimodel peak near +3.5°C.

coupling.name: Atmospheric Coupling
coupling.interp: Firmly established. SOI near −21 (Sep), Walker circulation markedly weakened; coupling carrying the event into its OND–NDJ peak.
